newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges stranded foreign truckers to seek aid.
newsitem.headline: France urges stranded foreign truckers to seek aid.

text.p: France on Tuesday voiced sympathy with foreign truckers stranded by their French colleagues' protests and offered tips on how to claim compensation.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said government officials had been instructed to monitor the plight of foreign drivers caught in the nine-day-old roadblocks and ensure their safety.
A German driver was seriously injured when strikers stoned his truck near the eastern town of Chalon-sur-Saone on Monday.

"We regret the consequences of these social protests on foreign hauliers," he told a news briefing. French truckers are blocking roads and fuel depots around the country to demand wage hikes, retirement at 55 and shorter working hours.
The blockade has left thousands of foreign truckers trying to drive through France between northern and southern Europe stranded and penniless.
Britain and Spain have protested to Paris, voicing concern over the financial damage suffered by small haulage companies from perishable cargoes and loss of earnings.

The French truckers have blocked the Channel ports of Calais and Boulogne -- major routes for ferries to Britain. Problems for British drivers have been exacerbated by the closure of the Channel Tunnel last week due to a fire.
Most European governments seemed sympathetic to the predicament of the Paris government, which is mediating in the talks between the strikers and their employers.

Rummelhardt said that up to 1,500 of the thousands of foreign lorry drivers, most of them British, finding themselves on French soil had been allowed to slip through roadblocks at the weekend with the help of local authorities.
He said foreign haulage companies should address compensation claims to the prefect, the local government representative in the region where their trucks were stranded.

They should list the dates and circumstances, provide evidence that the damage they suffered was abnormal and a direct consequence of the blockade, and attach accounting documents to assess the losses suffered.
Rummelhardt said hauliers could appeal in courts if the prefect rejected their claim.
